item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime V2 Improves Session Startup and Billing
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime V2 Improves Session Startup and Billing

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime provides a fully managed, serverless environment where each session runs in its own isolated microVM, scales to zero when idle, and you only pay for the resources your sessions consume.

🔍 Overview

  • AgentCore runtime runs each session in a new microVM.
  • The platform scales to zero when there’s no work and charges only for consumed resources.

🧩 How V2 Starts a Session

  • Setting platformVersion to “V2” changes how sessions start.
  • When you create or update a runtime, AgentCore starts your container in a fresh microVM and waits for the first healthy ping (GET /ping) within 120 seconds.
  • It then clears the operating system’s file cache, freezes the microVM, and stores its memory and disk as a snapshot. Building this snapshot takes a few minutes during create or update.

⚙️ Session Execution

  • On a new session, AgentCore restores the snapshot into a new microVM.
  • Your process resumes exactly where it was frozen, with imports, objects, and clients in place.
  • Files from the image are loaded lazily; each block is fetched the first time a session reads it and then cached closer to the host.
  • Anything held at snapshot time, including RAM‑backed file systems such as /dev/shm, is available at memory speed from the first access.
  • The file cache is cleared before the freeze, so reads during init do not speed up restored sessions.
  • A CLI that runs as a separate process and exits, or a browser binary, is read during init and then fetched again from the image for each restored session.

🚀 Performance Benefits

  • Session start times are faster and more consistent.
  • V2 reclaims memory that sessions don’t use, so billing tracks what the agent actually uses.
  • For most agents, switching to V2 is all it takes.

📏 Measuring Startup Time

  • AgentCore publishes CloudWatch metrics in the AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore namespace.
  • Latency: time to first byte.
  • OverheadLatency: platform overhead such as microVM start and snapshot restore on a new session.

🛠️ Tips for Agents

  • With the AgentCore Python SDK, init means everything before app.run().
  • If you run your own HTTP server (Node.js or another language), report healthy only after your initialization finishes.
  • Build hooks are now supported to keep work off the first request.

#AmazonBedrock #AgentCore #Serverless

Source: Architecture patterns for fast session startup on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Event‑Driven Sync of MCP Server Tools to AWS Agent Registry
item.description:
Event‑Driven Sync of MCP Server Tools to AWS Agent Registry

When a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server published in the AWS Agent Registry gains a new tool or updates its schema, the registry record is automatically refreshed via an event‑driven workflow.

🔍 Overview

  • An MCP server published in the AWS Agent Registry must keep its tool or schema record up‑to‑date.
  • An event‑driven workflow uses AWS CloudTrail, Amazon EventBridge, and AWS Lambda to automate the update.
  • The solution works in both single‑account and multi‑account environments.

🏗️ Architecture

  • AWS CloudTrail – captures UpdateAgentRuntime API calls as management events.
  • Amazon EventBridge – routes matching events to a Lambda function; supports cross‑account forwarding.
  • AWS Lambda (sync function) – queries the MCP server, diffs the tool list against the registry, and updates the record when needed.
  • AWS Agent Registry – stores MCP server records and their tool schemas as the source of truth.
  • AgentCore Identity – brokers OAuth token exchanges so the Lambda can authenticate without storing secrets.
  • Account roles
    • Account A (registry account) owns the Agent Registry, EventBridge rule, sync Lambda, and CloudTrail logs.
    • Account B (MCP server account) hosts the MCP server runtime and the Amazon Cognito OAuth provider.

⚙️ How It Works

  1. A developer updates an MCP server in Account B; the server calls the UpdateAgentRuntime API (via AgentCore CLI or directly).
  2. CloudTrail in Account B records the call as a management event (≈ 5–15 min delay).
  3. EventBridge in Account B captures the CloudTrail event and forwards it to the default EventBridge bus in Account A (cross‑account rule when applicable).
  4. The EventBridge rule in Account A triggers the sync Lambda, passing the full CloudTrail event JSON.
  5. The Lambda extracts the runtime Amazon Resource Name (ARN) from the event and builds the MCP server’s invocation URL.
  6. The Lambda obtains a secure OAuth bearer token through AgentCore Identity.
  7. The Lambda calls the MCP server (initialize, then tools/list) to retrieve the latest tools information.
  8. The Lambda locates the corresponding registry record by ARN, compares the retrieved schema with the stored one, and updates the record if a change is detected.
  9. The process assumes the registry already contains a pre‑registered record for the MCP server; the Lambda updates existing records only and does not create new ones.

🚀 Availability

  • The same workflow runs unchanged in a single‑account deployment where the registry, Lambda, EventBridge rule, and MCP server all reside in Account A.
  • In a multi‑account deployment, runtime events flow securely from Account B to Account A before the Lambda performs the sync.

#AWS #AgentRegistry #EventBridge #Lambda #MCP

Source: Automating AWS Agent Registry updates with push-based architecture | Amazon Web Services
